I like the demo and teaser for that they complete the story and motive for the Shogun. If it's only for "avoiding exceptions and pursue eternity", then she couldn't make the choice for all her people because there're ones who're willing to die for their ambitions. This, together with the teaser, conveyed another concept, that she believes in "emptiness" (寂), it's translated as "reality" in English but in Chinese or Japanese the meaning is closer to emptiness, nothingness, which is a deeply rooted concept in Zen and Buddhism. 

Basically, after losing her friends, who died directly or indirectly from their ambitions, she came out with a two-folded way of coping this. First, all fantasy and happiness are illusions, and it's ok (even natural) for me to lose them all, and the true reality is just emptiness and loneliness. Second, yet since me in the past have been and my people will be bothered by the loss of such illusion, I will put a stop to this cycle. 

Her sitting position, the lotus position with one leg down, is also a position seen in Buddhism statues in 400-600 China, from where Buddhism further spread to Japan. The meaning of "emptiness" in context of Buddhism says all fantasy are just emptiness and buried in emptiness there's the true reality, which echoes her quote very well.

The beginning of this trailer has a crow perched on Yae’s arm, which is how the end of the trailer ties to the beginning. Yae sends the crow flying away towards Tenshukaku as she explains the “lofty abode of the Raiden Shogun” (referring to the place the crow is flying to). Yae talks about how Raiden looks at the people and world below her (literally and figuratively) to see “a world mired in impermanence”. These are fancy words in which I shall let myself explain, if you’ll let me do the favor. To be “mired” means to be stuck, usually meant to mean “to be stuck in thick mud” but it can also mean “to be stuck” in the general sense or “to be held back” or “trapped”. “Impermanence” describes “noun: the state or fact of lasting for only a limited period of time” (-Dictionary). To literally translate into common words, the Raiden Shogun believes that her people and humanity as a whole are held back by the things that don’t last forever, the things that change and disappear. She uses her powers of lightning and thunder to “rule over transience”. Transience, being another word for “lasting for a short time”. It can also refer to the transitional state of something, or something that is undergoing change. Of course, all of these things are opposites to eternity, so Ba’al uses her lightning to subjugate and conquer transience, which has succeeded in keeping Narukami the same as it always has been for hundreds of years.

The Raiden Shogun believes that to yearn for something new is trivial and that to be passionate is petty. She wants to pursue an eternity that has no bars or chains, an eternity that will forever not be disturbed, never changing. (That is what “unfettered” and “unperturbed” literally means. Unrestricted and undisturbed). Due to my life experiences, I cannot agree with the Raiden Shogun. But at the same time, I believe that beneath her emotionless nature and underneath all of her actions is a genuinely good heart. I understand why she does the things she does. War and destruction, the result of change and angry passion. That is what brought death and loss both to a lot of the people of Inazuma in the past as well as what brought death to the Raiden Shogun’s closest friends, what brought loss to her. Change has only brought pain and sorrow, therefore she only sees change as a bad thing. Change brings pain wherever it goes. But that’s the thing, that’s the natural order. Change is a part of life. There is a certain kind of happiness that you can only get from pain and loss and the only way that you can feel sorrow is if you once knew what it was like to be happy. Sorrow comes when you feel like happiness has been taken away from you and sorrow is what also makes a special kind of happiness. Happiness and sorrow aren’t separate entities, they are woven into each other. If you strip away change and eternity becomes a true forever, sure, you won’t have any more pain, but happiness becomes harder to come by if at all. You strip away the meaning of life. Is removing all pain worth it when you remove the happiness that comes with it? I can sympathize with the Raiden Shogun, I have also been through pain and loss. Her pursuit of eternity is her way of coping with her grief.

I want to point out the music in this part of the trailer. It starts with a lone flute that states the main motif for Inazuma, a soft opener. The violin ensemble enters to build up an epic tension. And when you hear the brass that continues that motif, it is such a good way to build up this epic feeling. The recognizable part of the motif that the brass plays consists of four consecutive notes with two sets, the second set having the last two notes being raised slightly in relation to their original placement. At the very end of the second set that the brass instrument plays, when the violin ensemble gets more prominent, the camera zooms towards the Raiden Shogun who notices said camera as it fixes on her as it goes above Tenshukaku and to the other side of it and pans down to the cliffside, the camera now completely upside down. The violins in this section are gorgeously ominous and epic as hell because it’s the Raiden Shogun’s theme (you hear the motif when Ba’al stops the Traveller from untying Thoma and steps down with Electro energy as she refers to the Traveller’s ability to manipulate the elements).

The camerawork is really stunning and is one thing that you can really only manipulate to high extents in animation, 2D and 3D, since all you need is an idea, no drones or stunt actors. The way how the camera sort of follows the crow and flies above Inazuma City with it and pans over to a somewhat close-up shot of the Raiden Shogun. This sort of thing would be highly impressive if it was done with no special effects as a transition would likely be required plus coordination from the actor, but now I’m getting off-track. But I can’t help myself! The camera going into the ground and transitioning to the Plane of Euthymia, where we see the Raiden Shogun once again in the distance, with the stone Torii gates blocking our view to make seamless transitions to shots that bring the zoom closer to Ba’al. We see that ominous crimson moon behind Ba’al as she opens her eyes to acknowledge the presence of the camera, only for the video to reveal that this was actually a reflection against the fuller of Ba’al’s tachi which is ANOTHER great transition. And when she strikes the sky and summons a thunderstorm, the lightning bolt and Tenshukaku splits the middle of the screen, the mountains of Narukami Island on the right side and the ocean leading to the rest of the world to the left side. Not only does this symbolize the Raiden Shogun’s will to close off the nation from the rest of the world (the lightning, storms, and Tenshukaku all being symbolic of her power), it’s also a symbol of duality (you’re going to notice this theme of duality a *lot* throughout this analysis).

We’re only 50 seconds in and I made 4 paragraphs for this analysis. This is going to be a long one. There are no TL;DR’s.
I love the sound effect they use during the lightning strike scene above Tenshukaku. There is this sound effect that sort of sounds similar to a bullet hitting or ricocheting off of a metal slab or metal object that is a classic sound effect from Western cowboy films. Of course, that context doesn’t apply here, I just personally really like the use of the sound effect because it fits. I also wanted to point something out visually. There is this flash of white light that consists of a circle and a star-shape pointing in the cardinal directions (an artistic way to emphasize a bright light in animation), and after that flash you see two rainbows that make a circle to either side of the Raiden Shogun. Once again, duality, and the reason why there are rainbows is because there is rain acting as prisms to refract the light coming from the lightning because there is a thunderstorm oh my god THE DETAILS DON’T STOP! MIHOYO PLEASE LET ME SLEEP.
Ahem…

The eye of Ba’al’s Elemental Skill acts as a transition to Ba’al’s character portrait screen. “Raiden Shogun” flashes onto the center of the screen briefly before the name is laid out at the bottom of the screen (it’s decisions and touches like that which you notice but don’t think about too much that help make this trailer). Notice, very briefly, to the left and right in the background are two Raiden Shogun’s. When they disappear, the deep red from the Plane of Euthymia washes over the background as a stone Torii gate from the Plane appears to Ba’al’s right (your left). Her charged attack acts as a transition to the gameplay showcase portion of the trailer. In this specific moment a rectangle frame of Ba’al cuts in and immediately returns back to the original footage, now being washed over by a deep shade of blueish purple which acts as the transition to Ba’al attacking the Mirror Maiden. Again, another brief cut that you don’t have time to think on. The video doesn’t let you latch onto an idea and think on it for a while when it doesn’t want you to. You just see Ba’al and aspects of her condensed into a fast-paced well-edited video. The next cut in this time flashes by tons of images. In each of these cut-ins the border is always decorated with some kind of purple flower. For your information, I’m the kind of person who wants to be as factual as possible but I don’t have the energy to do extensive and deep research on the internet, so I don’t know if this is a specific real flower with some kind of symbolic meaning.

That said I do want to point out with each frame that the images change, the way the flowers are assorted also change. The editors and the people who directed the trailer didn’t need to add that touch, they could’ve easily just had the exact same drawing of the same assortment of flowers decorate the border of all the frames but they had the flowers drawn differently for a lot of the frames JUST for half a second of footage. Can I also point out how the majority of these cut-in frames are CLEAN desktop wallpaper material? Sheesh, miHoYo goes hard on everything. The way how the camera rotates and flies into the eye behind Ba’al which goes into footage of Ba’al fighting another Mirror Maiden. Smooth rotation is something used fairly often in this character demo. Check the next effect they do. The ring that appears behind Ba’al when she uses her Elemental Skill is showcased here and it is shown gradually lighting up. If you go frame by frame you’ll notice bolts of electricity emanating from the eye and striking some of the lights. Seriously who is in charge of the visual effects? Hats off to them. The camera sort of violently rotates and now you’re really noticing the thematic pattern here. Perfect rotation isn’t exactly deeply related to anything about Ba’al (from what I can discern) but in terms of video editing, having a consistent visual theme be it with the effects, how they move and how the camera is used to provide a visual sensation to the watcher is very important. The main thing here is consistency (I told you I would mention this later).

Consistency consistency consistency. It’s a very important thing when making a story, making character designs, making music. Sure you can make something that is literally about inconsistency but that in and of itself has some level of consistency, because if you just make something incoherent with no discernible meaning then there isn’t a point to the incoherency. Art of all types needs something to blend and tie things together. A story is unsatisfying without a conclusion befitting the nature of the story, and even before that point a story can be unsatisfying if you set the story up to make it sound like a fantasy epic in the prologue and then in chapter 1 it’s a slice of life story where nothing bad happens. Chapter 3 we are now exploring an unrelated adventure involving the side characters and chapter 5 is a sitcom (I mean if you’re really creative and you use some kind of consistency then a crazy story like that could work but that’s besides the point). What’s true about this analogy is also true for visual effects, editing, and a lot of other art.

When the ring cuts back in again it’s smoothly rotating to showcase an Electro symbol lighting up as it did in the last cut-in. The last time we see the ring in this section it is fully lit up. And then the music takes a slow turn and this transition is signaled by the screen going into a sort of monochrome black and white. The middle of the screen is split as both sides turn black. You can interpret this as maybe a door or a gate opening, or maybe it’s just a visual effect the team making the trailer chose to draw attention to the Raiden Shogun appearing in the middle. Or you can take this as another duality symbolism as it sort of looks like two eyelids moving away from each other. Now look at Ba’al. Slow down the footage. I’m talking 0.25x playback speed. You see how she’s glitching? And notice how the second version of Ba’al appears from behind her all grayed out. As the camera rotates to put the other Ba’al into a better view, the previous Ba’al continues glitching, becoming grayed out and transparent, while the new Ba’al is gaining color. The previous Ba’al’s eyes weren’t glowing. The new one on the other hand does have glowing eyes. The previous Ba’al was holding her weapon. The new one isn’t. You can interpret this a lot of ways. My first thought when I rewatched the trailer and starting thinking out loud to myself in this section was that it’s almost as if the energy of the first Ba’al is being sucked out and transferred over into the new one. This scene could be implying some kind of dual mentality. It could be representative of Ba’al’s old self turning into her new self (but the duality between two versions of her is still prevalent throughout the rest of the trailer so a part of me somewhat doubts that this is Ba’al’s old self). This could just be a representation of Ba’al tapping into her Gnosis and Archon powers as evidenced with the glowing eyes and from the fact that the next part of the trailer literally showcases Ba’al’s Elemental Burst. Speaking of which…

I love the violins here when the camera pans over Musoujin Gorge. I also love how the first thing we see when we cut back into the overworld is this blue and gray foggy sky with electricity. Here’s a personal note, I love foggy and gray aesthetics. I love rain clouds and I really like seeing very tall industrial things reaching through gray clouds (the kind of stuff you would see in a Half-Life game or something out of Little Nightmares 2). I personally find the aesthetic really beautiful and calming but it can also be used to convey a sense of dread or existential loneliness. This is sort of removed from the analysis but I can’t help my feelings. I would like to note that the footage begins by making the camera pan from upside down, as if this were a continuation of the scene near the beginning of the trailer where the camera goes into the ground in the clip where Tenshukaku is upside down. Now we begin upside down and we travel through Musoujin Gorge to go right side up. The electricity coursing from the walls of the gorge are a really good touch since not only is the implication that the Raiden Shogun’s powers are strong enough to leave behind dangerous residue that has lasted for centuries very ominous and imposing, it looks as if the walls and stone themselves have been infused with Electro and are conducting the electricity through the air.

AND THEN we get to the part of the trailer I am stoked to talk about because the renditions and cut-ins here are particularly jaw-dropping. As we zoom in to Ba’al we get these really brief black and white impact/transitional frames that let the video cut to Ba’al’s Burst animation. Notice how there is a flash of red as she draws her sword. Also notice how the animation for the eye opening begins with a slash making a line of light from left to right before the eye opens. This left to right slash is from Ba’al’s perspective because the enemy would be seeing this from right to left because of how Ba’al draws her sword. This left to right motion is what transitions the Burst animation back into gameplay since the camera is going to be behind Ba’al. The fact that Ba’al slashes the eye open as if the eyelids were stuck together and the eye was blind might mean that Ba’al believes that the light from her lightning is what will guide the people of Inazuma to her ideal eternity (the Electro symbol, the symbol for Inazuma is what makes up the iris and pupil). Remember that red flash I mentioned earlier? Remember that, it’s important.

Once the eye disappears, the camera focuses on Ba’al. Again, there is a red flash before it recedes into purple. When Ba’al is holding her tachi to her right and the camera starts to rotate counter-clockwise around Ba’al, the screen turns red with the lightning being colored the same red. The scene transitions to the Raiden Shogun facing off against a single Kairagi. But as Ba’al performs an overhead up to down swing the footage seemingly begins to do a reverse. Another flash of red happens again. Since the footage has been reversed you would expect Ba’al to strike her sword downwards since miHoYo is pulling the same trick here that they did for Kazuha’s character demo. But your expectations are quickly subverted when instead of doing her up to down strike, she goes into her teleport attack animation instead and the camera zooms out to show that she is fighting two Kairagi to either side of her rather than a single one directly in front of her. If you went frame by frame when the red flashed, you would have noticed that the single Kairagi that Ba’al was fighting against disappeared, but you wouldn’t notice in normal playback because the camera immediately focuses onto Ba’al. miHoYo didn’t reverse and playback the same footage, it was a transition to a different fight. This is one of the most well-done transitions I have ever seen period AND IT DOES NOT STOP THERE.

After Ba’al does her attack animation the camera zooms back in really close to her. Another red flash happens and Ba’al does this attack where she rotates her entire body and the camera rotates to follow her making one of the most coolest camera following shots I have ever seen in, anything. This rotating camera follow sequence is yet again ANOTHER TRANSITION into a different battle. The one prior had a red Kairagi to Ba’al’s right and a blue one to her left. After the transition happens, the red one is the one to her left and the blue one is the one to her right. Frame by frame reveals that it might’ve not been a perfectly smooth transition as you can see the background scenery changing suddenly while the animation plays but that’s a flaw I can ignore because, on normal replay, you’re never going to notice that. The only reason why I ended up noticing it was because I was trying to figure out all of the cool and intentional details that I wouldn’t notice without a slow playback. The scene does another transition again when the red flashes and Ba’al sheathes her tachi. The scenery changed and the Kairagi are now gone. The first time you watched this trailer you probably never even thought that you were seeing transitions, this was just really cool camerawork when the actual genius laid in how multiple scenes were smoothly pieced together with animation and editing (I also love how the Raiden Shogun’s braided hair is glowing like how Venti’s and Zhongli’s hair do when they use their abilities, notably their Bursts. With the previous two Archons it would be hard to notice as they only happen in the Burst animation and Zhongli’s ponytail was hidden by the camera angle. Ba’al’s Burst lasts for a longer period beyond the animation and you are mostly seeing her from behind her back where her hair is, so it’s much more noticeable).

The last gameplay footage we see of the Raiden Shogun is of her using her Musou Isshin charged attack (at least I think it’s her charged attack. Could be her final basic attack animation) against three Kairagi. One ominous cut-in of Ba’al being surrounded by falling “dead” Visions implying the people she killed. I like how she’s standing on (what might be) the ocean she was standing on earlier before the stylistic silhouette cut-ins. The last touch to this trailer is this final animated cutscene. The Raiden Shogun rises into the air and you can see specks of purple light that almost look like embers rising up with her. Then there is this veil of lights that briefly surrounds Raiden and moves with her. One cool pose and some flashes and brief frames where everything is monochrome (which to me symbolizes her emotionless expression). She swings her tachi and literally commands lightning to rip up the ground and knock out 3 Kairagi enemies (which is a reference to the gameplay showcase, specifically the last clip where she defeats 3 Kairagi, though in the gameplay they numbered 1 red 2 blue whereas the cutscene had 2 red and 1 blue. Plus, the gameplay Kairagi were ghosts so… never mind). After the bandit samurai are defeated, the same crow from the beginning of the trailer comes back again to make the trailer come around in a full circle. The crow perches on Raiden’s arm and the trailer ends with a haiku by Ba’al (the syllables follow the 5 - 7 - 5 formula).

“Waking world, you seem”
“Woven from the stuff of dreams”
“All shall fade away”
I would like to note that in the Japanese version of this trailer, this isn’t a haiku. Rather, it’s a short poem called a “Waka” that’s a little longer than a haiku but it’s not 5, 7, 5. Credit to Isaac Suh in the comment section of the Japanese character demo. This is what the Japanese poem translates to (as per the information from Isaac. If the translation is rough then let me know, I don’t speak fluent Japanese);
“We refer to only the things we see while we are sleeping as dreams, but this futile world also doesn’t seem like the reality.” (The original poet apparently lost their loved ones and felt that the world was meaningless and made this poem with those feelings, so it fits the Raiden Shogun very well).
Essentially, both poems are conveying that reality feels the same as dreams because dreams are fleeting. If both are made of one in the same, then both will fade away. It encapsulates why the Raiden Shogun pursues eternity. She doesn’t want reality to feel like a fleeting ever-changing dream anymore.
I want to take the time to appreciate Ba’al’s voice actor, both the one in English and Japanese. The English voice has this mature-sounding powerful tone (especially when she says “Torn to oblivion”). As for the Japanese VA… come on, she voices Mei-senpai from Honkai 3rd Impact, of course I love the voice acting.

I may be wrong with how I interpreted her quotes, but maybe people can learn more about her by reading this.

*"Fantasy can only survive with an underlying reality. Reality is the stillness buried deep within the illusion. This is eternity."*
So, what I get is that Baal considers "fantasy" something that contrasts and complements "reality", yet "reality" is a limited world, something that we mortals make up on our minds. She's seeking to create a world in which its "reality" is based on "fantasy", therefore neverchanging. She calls this reality "eternity".

*"Waking world, you seem woven from the stuff of dreams. All shall fade away."*
I think that in this part, she's talking to "transience". "Transience" is the power of change, and change is made up of "dreams", aspirations and the like; making it the counterpart of "eternity". She's planning to eradicate completely this "waking world" in order to continue her pursue of eternity. I mean, she even tagged the traveler as an "exception (to eternity)". Kinds of connects, I guess?

For anyone wondering what euthymia means:

In psychiatry and psychology, euthymia is a normal, tranquil mental state or mood.

In those with bipolar disorder, euthymia is a stable mental state or mood that is neither manic nor depressive, yet distinguishable from the state of healthy people. Euthymia is also the “baseline” of other cyclical mood disorders like major depressive disorder (MDD), borderline personality disorder (BPD) and narcissistic personality disorder (NPD). This state is the goal of psychiatric and psychological interventions.

The word “euthymia” is derived from the Greek words “eu”, well, and “thymo”, soul or emotion. The word “thymos” also had four additional meanings: life energy; feelings and passions; desires and inclinations; and thought or intelligence. Euthymia is also derived from a verb, “euthymeo”, that means both “I am happy, in good spirits” and “I make others happy, I reassure and encourage”. This is the basis on which the first formal definition of euthymia was built.
